name: Reading Failure
goal: Read a traceback, locate the failing line, and isolate a fault without guessing.

description.what: What Python prints when a program goes wrong, how to read it, and how to corner a fault that prints nothing at all.
description.why: Every programmer's day contains failure, and a learner who cannot read an error message has to wait for somebody else to explain it - which is the whole difference between learning on your own and not.
description.enables: You will be able to take an unfamiliar failing program, say what broke and where, and narrow a silent wrong answer down to the line that causes it.
description.assumes: You can write and run a small program: names and values, whole numbers and text, `if` and `else`, and loops that count or build up a total.
description.assessed: You will read real tracebacks and say what they mean, and you will repair broken programs whose faults you were not told the shape of.

sections.title: Read It From The Bottom
sections.body:
When Python meets something it cannot do, it stops the program and prints a **traceback**: a report of exactly where it was when it gave up. It looks alarming and it is not - it is the most useful thing Python ever prints, and the answer to most of the questions a beginner asks is inside one.

Read it **from the bottom**. The last line is the **error type** and its message, and that tells you *what* went wrong. Above it sit the pieces of your program that were part-way through running, oldest at the top and newest at the bottom. Each of those pieces is a **frame**: a `File "...", line N` line saying where, and under it the line of code itself, with `^` marks beneath the part that failed.

The bottom frame is where Python stopped. The frame above it is the **caller** - the line that asked for that work. The mistake is often not in the bottom frame at all, but in the value a caller handed it, which is why you read the last line first and then walk upwards.

annotations.text: Where the program stops, so this becomes the bottom frame of the traceback.
The middle frame. It asked for the division, but it did not choose the 0.
This call works and prints. Failure comes second, not first.
The real mistake lives here - the 0 that eventually reached the division.

checkpoint.prompt: This program stops with an error. Type the **last line** of its traceback.
checkpoint.code:
runes = 4
print("Runes carved:", runes)
print("Each rune costs:", 12 / totl)
checkpoint.explain: The last line always carries the error type and the message, and this message quotes the unknown name straight back at you - a name nothing ever set is nearly always a typo. Reading downwards instead tempts you to stop at the `File` line, which says where Python was but never what it objected to.

sections.title: Broken Before It Starts
sections.body:
There are two kinds of failure, and telling them apart saves hours. A **syntax error** means Python could not make sense of the text of your program, so it refuses to run a single line of it. A **runtime error** means the text was understood and Python ran it, and something went wrong part-way through - so the output up to that point really happened.

The tell is the output. If nothing at all printed, not even a line you know comes first, it is a syntax error. If some output appeared and then a report of failure, the program ran and failed later. A syntax error also has no `Traceback (most recent call last):` heading and no frames, because there was no running program to report on.

Python points at the first place where the text stopped making sense. That is never *before* your mistake, but it can be *after* it: a bracket you never closed only becomes impossible on a later line, and a missing comma is noticed at the item after it. So when the reported line looks perfectly innocent, suspect the end of the line above.

annotations.text: Run it: this never prints. Nothing runs at all when the text cannot be understood.
The line Python reports. It is fine in itself - what is missing is the comma that should end it.
The line it was reading when it decided the one above could not work.
Never reached, and never even read properly.

checkpoint.prompt: This program is run. What appears before the report of failure? If nothing appears at all, type `nothing`.
checkpoint.code:
print("Opening the vault")
print("Counting coins"
print("Closing the vault")
checkpoint.explain: The unclosed bracket on line 2 makes the whole file impossible to understand, and Python reads the whole file before running any of it - so line 1 never gets its turn. Expecting `Opening the vault` first is the natural guess, and noticing that it is missing is how you recognise a syntax error without reading a word of the message.

sections.title: The Five You Will Actually Meet
sections.body:
Error types are not trivia. Each one names a different kind of mistake, so the type alone usually tells you where to look.

- **NameError** - you used a name Python has never been given. Nearly always a typo, or a line that sets the name sitting after the line that uses it.
- **TypeError** - the values are the wrong *kind* for the operation, such as adding text to a number.
- **ValueError** - the kind is right but the value itself is impossible. `int("seven")` really is text, but it is not text that spells a number.
- **IndexError** - you asked a **list** (a row of values written in square brackets) for a position it does not have. Positions start at 0, so a list of three items has 0, 1 and 2, and asking for 3 is one too far.
- **ZeroDivisionError** - you divided by zero. The zero is almost never written down; it arrived in a name from somewhere else.

The message after the colon is worth reading in full, because it usually names the offending value.

annotations.text: Three items, so the only positions that exist are 0, 1 and 2.
`len` gives the count, 3 - always one more than the largest valid position.
One too far. This raises IndexError: list index out of range.

checkpoint.prompt: Name the error type each of these raises. Spell them exactly as Python does.
checkpoint.explain: `int("twelve")` is given text, which is the right kind for `int`, so the complaint is about the value and not the kind - that is the pairing most often swapped. The list holds positions 0, 1 and 2 only, so 3 is out of range rather than the wrong kind of thing to ask for.

sections.title: Probing, Not Guessing
sections.body:
Plenty of faults raise nothing at all: the program finishes and the answer is simply wrong. There is no traceback to read, so you have to make the program tell you what it is doing, and the plainest tool is `print`.

A good probe prints a **label as well as a value**, so its output cannot be mistaken for anything else, and it goes where you hold an assumption - just before the suspicious line, or inside the loop you doubt. Then work in halves: check a value half way through, and whichever half disagrees with what you expected is the half worth opening. Change **one thing at a time**, run again, keep what worked. Two changes at once and a passing run tells you nothing about which of them mattered.

Before any of that, **reproduce**: find the exact input that fails, and fails every time. A fault you cannot summon on demand cannot be confirmed fixed, and "it seems better now" is not a fix. Take the probes out once you are done.
sections.code:
def cost(nights, rate):
    total = 0
    night = 0
    while night <= nights:
        print("probe: night =", night, "total =", total)
        total = total + rate
        night = night + 1
    return total


print(cost(3, 20))

annotations.text: The suspicious line. Does the loop stop where you think it does?
A probe, labelled. One line, and it answers the question outright.
Expected 60 for three nights at 20. The probe shows four passes, not three.

checkpoint.prompt: Put these into the order that corners a fault soonest.
fragments: find an input that fails every single time
print a labelled value half way through, to see which half is already wrong
change one thing in the half that disagreed with you
run the failing input again and confirm the answer is now right
checkpoint.explain: Reproducing comes first because every later step is measured against it: without a reliable failing input you cannot tell a repair from a coincidence. Probing before changing is what makes the change informed rather than a guess, and confirming last is what turns the guess into knowledge.

guided-practice.prompt: This program stops with an error. Type the **last line** of its traceback.
guided-practice.answer: TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
guided-practice.explain: `+` means join for text and add for numbers, and Python refuses to guess which you meant, so mixing the two is a TypeError rather than a quiet conversion. The tempting answer is ValueError, because `"12"` does look like a number - but nothing here was asked to interpret it, only to add it.
guided-practice.hint: Read the message as a sentence. What kind of value is on the left of the `+`, and what kind is on the right?

guided-practice.prompt:
Read this traceback and answer the three questions about it.

`Traceback (most recent call last):`
`File "ledger.py", line 14, in <module>`
`print(summary(coins, holders))`
`File "ledger.py", line 10, in summary`
`return "Each: " + str(share(coins, holders))`
`File "ledger.py", line 6, in share`
`return coins / holders`
`ZeroDivisionError: division by zero`

steps.label: the line number where the program actually stopped
the line number that began the whole chain

guided-practice.explain: The bottom frame is the newest, so line 6 is where Python gave up, while line 14 at the top is the call that set everything in motion. Reading top-down invites you to name line 14 as the failure, and it is not - though it is very likely where the zero came from.
guided-practice.hint: Most recent call last. Which frame, then, is the most recent one?

guided-practice.prompt: This program stops with an error. What does it print **before** the report of failure?
guided-practice.code:
print("Opening ledger")
totals = [40, 30, 20]
print("Entries:", len(totals))
print("Fourth entry:", totals[3])
print("Closed")
guided-practice.explain: This file is understood, so it runs, and everything before the bad line really happened - that partial output is your evidence that the first lines were fine. `Closed` never appears, because a runtime error stops the program where it stands rather than skipping the offending line.
guided-practice.hint: A runtime error stops the program at that point. What had already run by then?

guided-practice.prompt: This program stops with an error. Type the **last line** of the message.
guided-practice.explain: There is no `Traceback` heading and no frame here, because nothing ran - the text could not be turned into a program in the first place. Expecting a traceback is the usual mistake, and its absence is itself the clue that the fault is in the text rather than in any value.
guided-practice.hint: What does every `if` line need at the end of it?

guided-practice.prompt: `greeting(name)` should give back the name with a title in front of it, so `greeting("Mara")` gives `"Adept Mara"`. Running it raises `NameError: name 'nmae' is not defined`. Repair it.
guided-practice.explain: A NameError message quotes the exact name Python could not find, so it hands you the typo directly: `nmae` appears once and nothing ever set it. The tempting repair is to create a name called `nmae`, which silences the message and answers a question nobody asked.
guided-practice.hint: The message names the unknown word. Compare it letter by letter with the name the function was given.

guided-practice.prompt: `label(count)` should give back a sentence such as `"You carry 3 coins"`. It raises `TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str`. Repair it so the sentence comes back for any whole number.
guided-practice.starterCode:
def label(count):
    return "You carry " + count + " coins"
guided-practice.solution:
def label(count):
    return "You carry " + str(count) + " coins"
guided-practice.explain: The message says which kind was unexpected and where: a number turned up on the right of a `+` whose left was text. Turning the text into a number instead would raise ValueError on `"You carry "`, which is the wrong end of the same problem.
guided-practice.hint: One of the three pieces being joined is not text. Which conversion makes it text?

guided-practice.prompt: `cost(nights, rate)` should give back the price of a stay, so three nights at 20 is 60. It gives 80. A probe inside the loop printed `night = 0`, `night = 1`, `night = 2` and `night = 3` before it finished. Repair it.
guided-practice.starterCode:
def cost(nights, rate):
    total = 0
    night = 0
    while night <= nights:
        total = total + rate
        night = night + 1
    return total
guided-practice.solution:
def cost(nights, rate):
    total = 0
    night = 0
    while night < nights:
        total = total + rate
        night = night + 1
    return total
guided-practice.explain: The probe output is the whole diagnosis: four values printed where three nights were paid for, so the loop runs once too often, and the condition is the only thing that decides that. Taking a quarter off the total would also give 60 for this input and be wrong for every other one - the probe is what tells you which repair is the real one.
guided-practice.hint: Count the probe lines. How many nights was it asked for, and how many did it charge for?

guided-practice.prompt: Someone tells you: "your program crashed yesterday, it was doing the totals wrong." Say what you need to establish before you change a single line, and why starting with a change is a mistake.
guided-practice.explain: Without a failing input you can summon at will, there is no way to tell a repair from a coincidence, and a good share of reported faults turn out to be a different input, a different program, or correct behaviour that surprised somebody. Changing code first also spends your evidence: if the failure stops appearing you will never know whether your change was the reason.
guided-practice.hint: You want the exact input, the exact output they saw, the output they expected, and the message itself.

independent-practice.prompt: `average_score(total, players)` should give back the average score per player, and should give back 0 when there are no players at all. At the moment it stops with an error in that case. Make it behave.
independent-practice.starterCode:
def average_score(total, players):
    return total / players
independent-practice.explain: Nothing is wrong with the division itself; the fault is that one particular value is allowed to reach it, so the repair belongs before the division rather than inside it. Note that no players and a total of zero are different cases - only one of them is a problem, which is why both are tested.

independent-practice.prompt: `third_item(values)` should give back the third item of `values`. It survives longer rows of values and fails on one of exactly three items, which is the case it exists for. Correct it.
independent-practice.explain: Positions are counted from 0, so the third item sits at 2 and the code was quietly reading the fourth - which is why a longer row hid the fault and the shortest one exposed it. An IndexError that appears on some inputs and not others is nearly always this off-by-one rather than a damaged row of values.

independent-practice.prompt: `is_ready(charge)` should give back `True` once the charge has reached 100 and `False` while it has not. Nothing runs at all at the moment - not one line of it. Get it working.
independent-practice.starterCode:
def is_ready(charge)
    if charge >= 100
        return True
    return False
independent-practice.explain: Nothing running at all, with no frames reported anywhere, places the fault in the text rather than in any value - so no amount of thinking about charges would have helped. Python reports only the first such fault it meets, so repairing one and running again is expected to reveal the next.

independent-practice.prompt: `highest(values)` should give back the largest number in `values`. On some rows of numbers it is right and on others it is wrong, and it never reports anything. Find where it goes astray and correct it. You may assume `values` always holds at least one number.
independent-practice.explain: The starting value is an assumption in disguise: it claims the answer is at least 0, which is true of many rows of numbers and false of any row that lies entirely below zero. Printing `best` on each pass shows it never moving, which points at the start rather than at the comparison - and a fault that appears on some inputs and not others is nearly always an assumption like this one.

independent-practice.prompt: A forty-line program reports a total that is far too large. Nothing fails, and reading it through twice has told you nothing. Describe how you would corner the fault, and say why altering three suspicious lines at once and running it again would leave you no wiser.
independent-practice.explain: Checking a value half way through splits the search rather than scanning it, so each look rules out a whole stretch of the program instead of a single line. Three changes at once destroys that: a run that suddenly behaves tells you the fault is gone but not which change removed it, and two of the three may have introduced faults that have not shown themselves yet.

exam.prompt: In a traceback, which line carries the error type and its message?
choices: the first line, `Traceback (most recent call last):`
the line with the `^` marks under it
exam.explain: The heading only announces that a traceback follows, and the frames say where Python was - the verdict itself is always the final line. Reading from the top is the habit that makes tracebacks feel unreadable.

choices: a fault found while the program is running, when a value turns out to be impossible
a fault in the text of the program, found before any line of it runs
any error serious enough to stop the program
a wrong answer produced by a program that ran to the end
exam.explain: The distinction is when the fault is found, not how serious it is: the text is read in full before anything runs, so a syntax error costs you the whole program rather than only the line it sits on. The third choice conflates the two kinds, which is the confusion that leaves people hunting for values that never existed.

exam.prompt: This program stops with an error. Type the **last line** of its traceback.
exam.answer: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'seven'
exam.explain: `int` is perfectly happy to be handed text - that is its job - so the kind is right and the complaint is about this particular value, which makes it ValueError rather than TypeError. The message quotes the offending value back at you, which is often the fastest route to where it came from.

exam.prompt: This program stops with an error. What does it print **before** the report of failure?
exam.code:
print("Start")
shares = 4
print("Shares:", shares)
shares = shares - 4
print(100 / shares)
print("End")
exam.explain: The zero is never written down anywhere - it arrives in `shares` one line before the division, which is the usual shape of a ZeroDivisionError. The partial output proves the first three lines behaved, so the search narrows to what happened between the last good print and the failure.

exam.prompt: Name the error type each of these raises. Spell them exactly as Python does.
exam.explain: `int("3 coins")` is the one people get wrong: it does begin with a digit, but `int` needs the whole of the text to spell a number, so the value is impossible rather than the wrong kind. `4 - 4` shows how a zero divisor usually arrives - computed, not typed.

exam.prompt: Put these into the order you read a traceback in.
fragments: the last line, for the error type and its message
the bottom frame, for the line that was running when it stopped
the frames above it, for who asked for that work and with what
the top frame, for where the whole chain began
exam.explain: Bottom-up is not a preference: the verdict tells you what kind of thing to hunt for, and only then is it worth knowing where. Starting at the top means reading frames while you still do not know what you are looking for.

exam.prompt:
Read this traceback and answer the questions about it.

`Traceback (most recent call last):`
`File "stock.py", line 20, in <module>`
`print(restock("crate", boxes))`
`File "stock.py", line 15, in restock`
`return describe(shelf_for(kind))`
`File "stock.py", line 9, in shelf_for`
`return SHELVES[kind_number]`
`IndexError: list index out of range`

steps.label: the name of the function the program stopped inside
the line number that called that function

exam.explain: The `in shelf_for` at the end of a `File` line names the function that frame belongs to, and the frame above it is its caller - so `kind_number` was decided at or above line 15. Naming line 9 as the caller is the usual slip: line 9 is the line that failed, not the line that asked.

exam.prompt: `sum_to(n)` should give back the total of every whole number from 1 to `n`, so `sum_to(4)` is 10. It gives 6. Repair it.
exam.starterCode:
def sum_to(n):
    total = 0
    step = 0
    while step < n:
        total = total + step
        step = step + 1
    return total
exam.solution:
def sum_to(n):
    total = 0
    step = 1
    while step <= n:
        total = total + step
        step = step + 1
    return total
exam.explain: Printing `step` on each pass shows the numbers actually added - 0, 1, 2, 3 - where the harmless 0 and the missing 4 together say the loop is one short at the top rather than wrong in the middle. Adding `n` to the answer at the end would also give 10 here and would be wrong for `sum_to(0)`, which is why that edge case is tested.
exam.hint: Which numbers does the loop actually add? Write them down for `n = 4`.

exam.prompt: A traceback ends with `ZeroDivisionError: division by zero`, and its bottom frame is a two-line function that does nothing but divide one number by another. Explain why the mistake is probably not in that function, and how the frames above the last line help you find it.
exam.explain: A function that only divides cannot be blamed for the numbers it was handed, so its frame is where the fault surfaced rather than where it was made. Every frame above names both a line and the call that line made, so walking upwards traces the offending value back to the place it was computed - and that is the line worth changing.
